title: The Periodic Table and Periodic Trends
seo_title: Periodic Table Worksheets: Groups, Valence Electrons and Trends (High School Chemistry)
standard_text: Use the periodic table as a model to predict the relative properties of elements based on the patterns of electrons in the outermost energy level of atoms.
meta_desc: Free high school chemistry worksheets on the periodic table (NGSS HS-PS1-1): groups and periods, families, valence electrons, ion charges and trends in radius, ionization energy and electronegativity. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Elements in a group react alike; size and pull on electrons follow clear trends.
body_html:
How to think about it

The periodic table is a map of outer electrons.

  • Groups (columns) share valence electrons, so they react alike. Periods (rows) = number of shells.
  • Down a group: atoms get bigger; ionization energy and electronegativity go down.
  • Across a period (left to right): atoms get smaller; ionization energy and electronegativity go up.
Example

Valence electrons in sulfur (group 16)?

16 − 10

Answer: 6

Example

Larger atom: lithium or cesium (same group)?

Cesium has more shells

Answer: cesium

Common mistakes

  • Thinking atoms get bigger from left to right.
  • Mixing up groups (columns) and periods (rows).
  • Thinking noble gases react easily.

faq.q: How do you find valence electrons from the periodic table?
faq.a: For groups 1 and 2, use the group number. For groups 13 to 18, subtract 10. Helium has 2.

faq.q: What are the main periodic trends?
faq.a: Atomic radius increases down a group and decreases across a period. Ionization energy and electronegativity do the opposite.

faq.q: Why do elements in the same group behave alike?
faq.a: They have the same number of valence electrons, and valence electrons control chemical reactions.
